title: The Saker and the Birds

full_text:
A fierce hunting saker—a falcon of great speed and deadly talons—grew weary of serving the royal falconer. One afternoon, breaking his silver jesses during a chase, he escaped into a tranquil valley where flocks of doves, linnets, and starlings lived in peaceful harmony.

Perching upon a flowering almond bough, the falcon smoothed his sharp plumage, softened his fierce yellow glare, and called out to the fluttering songbirds: 'O gentle birds of the grove, do not flee from me! For years I was compelled by human masters to hunt my feathered brethren, but my soul has turned from violence. I come to offer you my protection! With my wings to guard you, no hawk or serpent shall ever dare approach your nests.'

The young and inexperienced doves fluttered near, marveling at the falcon's majestic stature and soothing speech. 'How wonderful!' cooed a fledgling. 'The king of hunters has become our guardian!'

However, an elderly ringdove who had nested in the valley for ten summers perched safely upon a high thornbush and warned the flock: 'Stay back, my children! Judge a hunter by his nature, not by his afternoon sermon. When did the falcon's curved beak ever learn to crack millet seeds? When did those razor talons ever learn to cradle a fledgling without drawing blood?'

To test the falcon's sincerity, the old dove rolled a ripe fig along the branch toward the raptor: 'If you have truly joined our fellowship, O noble saker, partake of the fruit of the tree with us.'

The saker looked at the sweet fig with disgust, his sharp eyes flashing with suppressed hunger. Unable to contain his predatory instinct any longer, he lunged with outstretched claws to strike the old dove! But the cautious dove had anticipated the attack and dropped into the thorny thicket where the falcon’s broad wings could not follow.

The entire flock took wing and scattered into the safety of the rocky clefts, while the frustrated falcon flew away hungry. The birds praised the ancient ringdove, learning that honeyed promises cannot change the fangs of a predator.
moral: A reputation for cruelty cannot be undone by sudden words of friendship; true trust requires proven action.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Saker and the Birds"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.
